title: When Does a Frame Become an Outline?
selectionMethod: Internal 1-5 judgments in order: originality, visual necessity, interaction meaning, feasibility. Reasons, not totals, determine the choice. Scores are planning notes and are never displayed as evidence or outcomes.

hypotheses.idea: Contract a centered frame symmetrically around a fixed centered square until their edges coincide
hypotheses.reason: Selected: it follows Day025's unresolved resize operation while removing translated-frame asymmetry and keeping both square and frame centers fixed.

hypotheses.idea: Show only three fixed frame sizes around the same square
hypotheses.reason: A static triptych would preserve endpoint comparison, but it would not let the visitor inspect intermediate symmetric gaps or reset a chosen state.

hypotheses.idea: Toggle whether the coincident frame is painted above or below the square
hypotheses.reason: Layer order directly challenges edge ownership, but it introduces a second manipulated variable before the simpler geometric coincidence is documented.

hypotheses.idea: Morph a filled square into a stroked square while its outer dimensions stay fixed
hypotheses.reason: The transition would be visually direct, but changing fill into stroke changes the object itself rather than testing the relation between object and frame.

hypotheses.idea: Reveal a centered square through a shrinking mask
hypotheses.reason: Masking connects strongly to the current paper but changes visible area and occlusion, making it a poor test of symmetric frame distance.

hypotheses.idea: Pulse the frame between open and coincident states
hypotheses.reason: Animation would dramatize the switch but make timing and motion history unavoidable and produce an unequal reduced-motion alternative.

hypotheses.idea: Repeat the contraction with circles instead of squares
hypotheses.reason: Circles would avoid corners, yet they would break the explicit square-and-frame continuity before the resize confound from Day025 is tested.

hypotheses.idea: Contract a frame around a word until it touches the glyph bounds
hypotheses.reason: Typography could be meaningful later, but sidebearings, ascenders and word recognition add several contour systems to a still unresolved boundary question.

hypotheses.idea: Use a photograph and contract its crop frame toward one object
hypotheses.reason: A photograph would add semantic salience, texture, unequal edges and licensing concerns that prevent precise equality of the boundary conditions.

hypotheses.idea: Let four frame edges move independently toward the square
hypotheses.reason: Independent edges would reveal asymmetry, but the four-dimensional control would turn one visual question into a layout tool with many uncontrolled combinations.

variable: The adjustable frame's equal gap from the fixed square changes from 18% to 0% of field width, so its size changes from 66% to 30% while both centers remain fixed.
comparison: A persistent open endpoint and coincident endpoint flank one adjustable specimen. Every specimen contains the same centered 30% square; the frame alone changes size symmetrically.
constants: Same square size, position, color and orientation
Same field size, color, center and clipping
Same frame color, stroke treatment and center
No autoplay, stored response, score, external media or participant-data collection
challenge: If any apparent shift from container to outline is better explained by smaller enclosed area, orange-blue contrast, endpoint labels, panel order or the physical overlap of the stroke, or disappears when anchors reverse, do not attribute it to a general border-ownership change.
researchLedForm: Three simultaneous square fields avoid a memory-only comparison. The current border-ownership paper makes the boundary relation worth isolating, while the previous moving-frame limitation leads to a centered symmetric contraction. Malevich's White on White supplies a historical counterexample in which imprecise, low-contrast edges produce open space; today's exact contrasting edges deliberately test a different construction without reproducing the painting.
mediaDecision: Responsive HTML and CSS keep the square coordinates, frame inset and endpoints mathematically inspectable at every viewport. A still would remove reversible intermediate states; video would add timing; a photograph or generated image would add texture and resampling. Code-native geometry is therefore the necessary material, not a default preference.

revisits.question: Counterbalance anchor order, colors, labels and starting gap in a fixed viewport; ask container, outline, object and confidence as separate responses.
Compare translated frame, resized frame and mask conditions with matched endpoints and inspect design tools for explicit shared-edge or boundary-coincidence checks.
